context: marine-civil-led · breakwater & dredging protect the basin; floating pontoons carry the berths

brief.intro: New to this project type? A marina or waterfront development starts with marine civil works to create a sheltered, deep-enough basin — a breakwater to break incoming waves, dredging to reach design depth, and quay walls where the shoreline itself is the berth — before any pontoons go in. Most berths then float on pontoons anchored to piles or chains rather than sitting on a fixed deck, so they rise and fall with the tide, and every utility (power, water, fuel) has to reach a moving structure through flexible service risers. A small building (harbourmaster's office, clubhouse, fuel kiosk) and land-side parking round out the scope, but the real programme risk is the marine works — weather/tide windows, dredging permits and breakwater armour placement — plus proving the floating berths under a live load and mooring test.

glossary.plain: a rock or concrete barrier built to break incoming waves and shelter the marina basin.
removing seabed material to reach the design water depth vessels need.
a fixed vertical wall structure vessels berth directly against, as opposed to a floating pontoon.
a floating platform that rises and falls with the tide, carrying the actual berths.
how a floating pontoon system is held in place — either guided by fixed piles or held by anchors and chains.
the point on a pontoon where a berthed boat plugs into power and fresh water.
flexible cabling/piping that lets utilities follow a pontoon as it rises and falls with the tide.
a fixed point where a boat's sewage holding tank is emptied instead of discharged to sea.

must_get_right: Sequence the marine civil works first — breakwater and dredging must protect and deepen the basin before pontoons and quay walls can go in safely.
Plan pontoon utilities (power, water, fuel) as flexible, tide-following connections, not fixed building services — a rigid design assumption here causes rework.
Marine plant (dredger, piling rig, barge) is a scarce mobilised resource limited by tide and weather windows — protect its schedule like a long-lead item, not a generic subcontractor.
The pontoon/mooring load test and a live berthing/mooring trial are the real acceptance test, not architectural completion of the landside building.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Marine activities are durationed against marine-plant productivity rates (armour units or dredge volume per workable week), not generic civil productivity. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Marine works (breakwater placement, dredging, pontoon installation) run on a tide- and weather-dependent calendar with a modelled allowance for non-workable days by sea state and wind speed; landside works (building, parking) run a standard calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs marine mobilization → breakwater construction (in parallel with dredging) → quay wall / pontoon anchoring → berth utilities (flexible risers, shore power, water) → pontoon & mooring load test → live berthing trial → handover. The landside building and parking are typically not on the critical path.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Metocean and tide data validated at design; the marine plant spread is mobilised once for the duration of the marine works; a disposal site for dredged material is available and permitted; seabed and coastal conditions match the geotechnical/metocean investigation.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule is driven by marine-specific hardware and permitting. The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Marine plant (dredger, piling rig, barge) is a scarce, mobilised resource shared across the works; sea-state and weather windows constrain daily working hours; dredging permits and disposal-site availability gate dredging start; vessel and public access to the basin must be coordinated with the harbour authority throughout.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: weather/tidal downtime, dredging permit delay, marine plant unavailability, and pontoon/mooring delivery slippage. Schedule contingency is held around the breakwater/dredging fronts and again ahead of the pontoon/mooring load test, rather than spread thinly across the network.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the marine plant — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
